title: Accounting for yourself
hookLine: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account, a saying attributed to Umar

lines: BEFORE YOU ARE TAKEN TO ACCOUNT.
cards: A shopkeeper pulls down the shutters, sits on an upturned crate, and opens the ledger. What came in. What went out.
Who still owes, and whom he still owes. Nobody makes him do it. A shop that never counts finds out the truth all at once, on its worst day.
Muslim teachers of the inward path borrowed that ledger for the soul.
A saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, puts it in one breath: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account.

teach.b: The word is muhasabah: taking account, holding a reckoning with yourself. Umar's saying turns on one verb used twice. Hasibu, take account, and tuhasabu, be taken to account.

Once by you, gently and early, and once on a day you don't choose. The Qur'an gives the reason in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow."
Every day sends something ahead; muhasabah is looking at what went.

In the collection of al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that the wise one holds himself to account and works for what comes after death, and al-Tirmidhi records Umar's saying right alongside it.
Then al-Ghazali, in the Revival, makes it practical, and yesterday's word comes back. He pictures the soul as a business partner.
In the morning, you set the terms: today, this and not that. Through the day, you keep an eye on it. That's muraqabah.
At night, you check the accounts. That's muhasabah.
And a ledger has two columns. The evening accounting isn't a trial where you're found guilty every night. What's wrong goes to tawbah, the turning back from two days ago: regret it, stop, mend it.
What's right goes to thanks. A merchant who only reads the losses quits. A merchant who only reads the profits gets robbed.

how: Some Muslims who follow the teachings of the inward path set aside a few minutes at night to review the day, asking forgiveness for what went wrong and thanking Allah for what went right.

o: paying the yearly charity owed on your savings
a judge's ruling on a dispute between two merchants
taking account of yourself: the soul's evening ledger

games.q: the evening ledger — tap the pairs.
p: set the terms with the soul

s: muhasabah means punishing yourself for every mistake
the ledger has two columns: what's wrong goes to tawbah, what's right goes to thanks.
"take account of yourselves" is a verse of the Qur'an
it's a saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab, recorded by al-Tirmidhi.
al-Ghazali pairs watching by day with accounting at night
he pictures the soul as a business partner: terms in the morning, watching all day, accounts at night.

games.q: you're al-Ghazali's merchant. the shop is closed, and one deal today went badly. what do you do with the ledger?
o: leave it shut. tomorrow is a new day.
go line by line: mend the loss, give thanks for the gains.
tear out the bad page and keep the good ones.
games.why: the merchant checks the accounts every night. the losses go to tawbah, the gains to thanks. skipping either column is how a shop fails.

practice: Run back over today, from this moment to the moment you woke, like rewinding a film.

Let one entry stand out in the good column, a kindness, a prayer kept, a job done well, and one in the other, a word you'd take back, a thing left undone, and just name the two, with no verdict on yourself.
If you pray, say alhamdulillah for the first and astaghfirullah for the second; if you don't, simply hold both, side by side.

wordCard.voice: Muhasabah. Taking account of yourself, the soul's evening ledger, read in both columns before the final reckoning. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: taking account, holding a reckoning with yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: count before counted. Two columns, and you read both. Same time tomorrow.
